$schema.description: The authoring schema, for editor completion and validation. Nothing at runtime reads it.

version.description: Your own semver, display and identity only. The installed code's identity is the pinned commit sha.

category.description: Which section of the Extensions tab this sits under: a grouping by what it is FOR, which cannot be derived from what it contributes. A section this app has never heard of lands in 'Other' rather than failing to install.

art.description: This extension's own mark, as a complete SVG document inline: the tier an author controls fully. Give it a viewBox and let it fill its own square edge to edge; it is drawn as the tile, not as a glyph on a plate. Kept as readable SVG text (not base64) so a registry reviewer can see what they are publishing, drawn inert so it cannot script the page, and capped at 4 KB. Anything that does not parse as SVG falls back to `logo`, then `icon`, then initials.

logo.description: A simple-icons slug, fetched from a CDN: right for standing in for somebody else's product. Add a "/<hex>" suffix to force a colour for a mark that vanishes against the surface it lands on. Unreachable in an offline sandbox, so it falls back to `icon`, then to initials.

icon.description: A name from the host's own icon set, drawn when no simple-icons slug fits. It ships in the image, follows the theme and costs no request: what actually carries a first-party extension. An unknown name falls back to initials rather than to a hole.

engines.description: A semver range over the host's extension API version, checked before your code is activated.

entry.description: Repo-relative path of your prebuilt single-file ESM bundle, built with `vue` and `@intentic/extension-api` as externals. Absent ⇒ an extension with no UI.

power.sentence: runs a UI bundle in your browser

server.description: Repo-relative path of your prebuilt single-file node ESM server bundle, exporting `activateServer`. Served under your own route namespace, which the daemon proxies. Nothing is provided at runtime but node builtins, so bundle everything else in. Absent ⇒ no backend.

power.sentence: runs a backend bundle inside the daemon's extension host

permissions.description: How far this extension may reach into the daemon, as "<METHOD> <path-glob>" entries where `*` matches one path segment: e.g. "GET /panels", "POST /panels/*/start". The install dialog shows these, the host refuses anything undeclared, and the usage ledger records which were actually earned.

sandbox.description: Daemon routes your UI half may call. Your own backend namespace needs no entry: its backend is your own code.

power.sentence: its UI calls the sandbox route ${value}

daemon.description: Daemon routes your SERVER half may call. Separate from `sandbox` because the two halves run as different principals: the UI as the owner's session, the backend as a minted per-extension token, so a grant to one must never quietly widen the other.

power.sentence: its backend calls the daemon route ${value}

events.description: Events your backend hears through `api.events` beyond its settings and the workspace's changes: `run`, a turn ending in a conversation it started through POST /agent with its own token; `activity`, whether any agent turn is running in the sandbox.

power.sentence: its backend hears when a conversation it started finishes a turn
its backend hears whether any agent turn is running in the sandbox

work.description: Whether your backend may hold work in flight with `api.work.hold(label)`: while held, the sandbox stays awake and an update or restart waits for it, as for an agent's turn.

power.sentence: its backend keeps the sandbox awake, and a restart waiting, while it holds work in flight

exec.description: The workload classes `api.exec` may run a command under: `command`, admitted and ranked as an agent's shell command; `toolchain`, a heavy tool (a build, a test run, an analyser), which also takes turns in the sandbox's heavy-command queue.

power.sentence: its backend runs commands, admitted like an agent's
its backend runs heavy tools, queued with the sandbox's builds and tests

fires.description: Handlers an automation may fire in your backend (`api.automations.onFire(name, handler)`): an automation whose target is `{ kind: "extension" }` names this extension and one of these, and fires it on its trigger under the scheduler's admission, holds and journal, without an agent.

power.sentence: the sandbox's automations wake its backend's "${value}" handler

label.description: The name shown on the tile or tab. The manifest's value wins over the one passed at registration.

surface.description: Where it appears. `rail` is a tile in the global left rail; `directory` is a panel opened from a repo in the Workspace tree; `sandbox` is a tab on the Sandbox hub, for a view whose subject is the box rather than the work.

badge.description: Allow this view to say something on its tile: a count, a glyph, or that work is running there. Declared because a badge interrupts from every other screen in the app; leave it out and any badge the extension registers is dropped.

power.sentence: may badge the "${label}" tile from any screen
a ${surface} view "${label}"

views.description: Sidebar elements this extension may register at runtime. Each entry reserves an id and a surface; the extension supplies the component with api.views.register, and the host refuses any registration this list does not cover.

path.description: Workspace-root-relative, forward-slash, matched by prefix, so one entry covers an exact file (`.intentic/config/automations.json`), a directory (`.intentic/config/approvals/`, with the trailing slash so it cannot match a sibling file) or a name family (`.intentic/environment.`). Not a glob.

invalidates.description: The query keys this path makes stale, the first element of your own api.sandbox.key(...) keys. Keep both this and the path as narrow as the view actually needs: a broad prefix costs every connected browser a refetch on every matching write.

power.sentence: is told when ${path} changes

files.description: Which workspace files back your views, so the daemon's file watcher can tell the browser they went stale instead of you polling for it. The agent edits the workspace out of band from every HTTP route, and this push is the only thing that can notice.

extensions.description: Bare file extensions, no dot: e.g. ["docx", "xlsx"].

fetch.description: How much of the file the host hands you. `text` for a format that is text (svg, a subtitle track). `blob` for one that must be parsed end to end before any of it shows (a .docx, a spreadsheet), bounded by the daemon's raw-read cap. `url` for anything range-read rather than parsed (audio, video): your component gets a streaming URL to point an element at, never the bytes. `path` for a viewer whose own backend reads and writes the file: you get the workspace path and the scope it is viewed in, plus `readOnly` where the window may not write the file and, in a desktop app's local window, a `text` slot holding the document's text for while your own view can't show it. Emit `dirty` (a boolean) whenever you start or stop holding edits the file doesn't have, so a window closing over them can ask first.

edit.description: Whether this viewer writes the file back. An editing viewer is chosen over a render-only viewer claiming the same extension, whatever order the two activated in.

compare.description: Whether this viewer also draws two versions of a file as one, with what changed marked in place: its registration then carries a `compare` component the host renders with `before` and `after` blobs. Only for `fetch: "blob"`.

power.sentence: ${edit?opens and edits:opens}${compare? and compares:} .${extensions|, .} files (${fetch})

viewers.description: File formats this extension can render. The host resolves an opened file to your viewer by its extension, fetches the content, and renders your component with it: you keep none of the fetch lifecycle and none of the daemon credentials.

label.description: The family's name, shown in the install dialog beside your other contributions. Per-row wording stays with the provider, which is the only thing that knows what it found.

power.sentence: marks workspace directories ("${label}")

documents.description: Per-directory documents this extension can offer. Your provider marks the rows in the Workspace tree it has something to say about, and the host opens your component as a tab.

label.description: What one of these is called ("CI run"), shown in the install dialog and on a tab whose own title could not be read. Each tab's title is the extension's to say for the thing it shows.

links.description: Allow this side view to take links the chat renders: a link it recognises (its registration's `claim`) opens beside the chat instead of in a new browser tab. Declared because it changes what the reader's click does; leave it out and the host never asks.

power.sentence: opens links it recognises as "${label}" beside the chat
shows "${label}" in the side panel

sideViews.description: Things this extension can show in the editor's side panel, one input at a time, beside whatever the reader is doing. Each entry reserves an id; the extension supplies the component with api.sideViews.register and opens one with api.sideViews.open, and the host refuses any id this list does not cover.

title.description: What the command palette shows. The manifest's value wins over the one passed at registration.

category.description: What the command acts on ("Deployments", "Knowledge"), drawn ahead of the title as "Category: Title" and searched with it. Use the extension's own name so its commands group together; omit it and the command stands alone.

icon.description: A name from the host's icon set, drawn beside the title.

keybinding.description: A global keyboard shortcut, e.g. "Mod+Shift+K" — `Mod` is ⌘ on Apple and Ctrl elsewhere. Declared here because a global shortcut is consequential: the owner approves it at install, and the host binds only what was approved.

power.sentence: the global shortcut ${keybinding} ("${title}")

mac.description: The shortcut on a Mac, where it differs from `keybinding`, e.g. "Mod+Alt+K" for a `keybinding` of "Ctrl+Shift+K". Without one, a Mac uses `keybinding` too. A Mac's text fields answer ⌃A, ⌃E, ⌃K, ⌥←/→ and ⌘←/→ themselves, so the host never binds those from a field whatever is declared.

power.sentence: the global shortcut ${mac} on a Mac ("${title}")

when.description: When the shortcut applies, as a condition over the shell's context keys, `tabSurface == 'chat'`, `!editableTarget`. Without one the chord is claimed everywhere, including inside a terminal where a bare key belongs to the program running in it. The command palette ignores this: a command is always runnable by name.

power.sentence: a palette command "${title}"

commands.description: Commands this extension may register handlers for, surfaced in the command palette. Title, icon and shortcut all come from here rather than from the registration call, because this is what the owner approved at install.

type.description: Which control the Settings page draws. `enum` reads its choices from `enum`.

enum.description: The choices, for type "enum". Meaningless otherwise.

enumItemLabels.description: What each choice in `enum` is called on the Settings page, by position. A choice without one shows its value.

enumDescriptions.description: One line under each choice in `enum`, by position: what picking it means. With these the Settings page lists the choices with their lines instead of a dropdown, so keep `description` for what holds whichever is picked.

secret.description: Mask the value in the UI and strip it from reads: a set secret round-trips as 'still set', never as its value.

env.description: Inject the stored value into the agent's shell environment under this name, every turn. How a credential you hold reaches the agent's command-line tools.

power.sentence: puts the "${key}" setting into the agent's environment as ${env}

settings.description: Typed settings the host renders into the Settings page for you and persists daemon-side. You never draw the form or store the value; you read it back with api.settings.get.

cwd.description: Relative to the extension checkout. Absent ⇒ the checkout root.

port.description: Assign a free port and inject it as PORT.

preview.description: Expose the port on a tunnelled preview hostname.

autoStart.description: Launch it on install and on daemon boot, rather than waiting to be started.

power.sentence: a background process "${name}"${autoStart? (starts on boot):}

processes.description: Long-lived background processes the daemon runs for this extension: a gateway holding a connection the daemon must not, a dev server. Managed the same way panel dev servers are, and startable and stoppable from the Extensions tab.

path.description: Relative to the extension checkout. Absent ⇒ the checkout root.

power.sentence: contributes skills, agents and hooks to the agent's turns

agent.description: Declare that this checkout is also a Claude Code plugin, so Claude Code turns pick up its skills, agents, hooks and commands. Only Claude Code reads it: give the agent tools with `contributes.tools`, which every runtime gets, and put a skill every runtime should read in a capability card's `skill`. MCP servers in the plugin's `.mcp.json` are deprecated, reach Claude Code alone, and are warned about at load.

fragment.description: Checkout-relative path to a file holding ONLY RUN and ENV instructions. FROM and privileged directives are rejected: those stay daemon-owned.

power.sentence: bakes an environment fragment into the sandbox image

environment.description: A Dockerfile fragment baked into the sandbox image so your tools are actually installed at runtime: a whisper binary, a psql client. The owner approves the composed overlay and rebuilds out of band, so this does not take effect immediately.

art.description: This extension's own mark, as a complete SVG document inline: the tier an author controls fully. Give it a viewBox and let it fill its own square edge to edge; it is drawn as the tile, not as a glyph on a plate. Kept as readable SVG text (not base64) so a registry reviewer can see what they are publishing, drawn inert so it cannot script the page, and capped at 4 KB. Anything that does not parse as SVG falls back to `logo`, then `icon`, then initials.

logo.description: A simple-icons slug, fetched from a CDN: right for standing in for somebody else's product. Add a "/<hex>" suffix to force a colour for a mark that vanishes against the surface it lands on. Unreachable in an offline sandbox, so it falls back to `icon`, then to initials.

icon.description: A name from the host's own icon set, drawn when no simple-icons slug fits. It ships in the image, follows the theme and costs no request: what actually carries a first-party extension. An unknown name falls back to initials rather than to a hole.

description.description: ONE LINE: aim for 60 characters or fewer. The grid clamps it at two lines in a narrow pane, so a paragraph here is a paragraph the reader gets truncated. Everything longer belongs in `hint`.

hint.description: The paragraph, shown under the add form and searched from the catalog, so the words that identify this card to someone hunting for it ("webauthn", "socket mode") belong here even when the tile cannot show them.

guide.description: The walkthrough the install dialog renders for getting the credential this card asks for.

links.description: Links each connected card of this kind offers on its row, for a step taken on the service's own site after connecting (inviting a bot to a server). A template naming a secret field is refused: the editor is never shown one.

label.description: What the link says on the connected card: "Add to your server".

url.description: The address, templated over the card's non-secret fields like `env`: `${field}` substitutes, `${field:uri}` percent-encodes. Offered only once every field it names holds a value.

secret.description: Mask it, and never echo it back.

advanced.description: Fold this field behind the form's Advanced disclosure: for answers whose default is right for nearly everyone. The disclosure opens by itself while any advanced field holds a non-default value, so an edit never hides live settings.

boolean.description: Render it as a switch, carrying "on"/"off". For an opt-in EXTRA rather than a decision: a two-option picker says the same thing but presents a choice the user must make to proceed, sized like the required fields around it. A switch always holds a value, so a field like this never blocks a submit.

hint.description: Shown on hover behind an (i) beside the label, never as text under the control: for what the label alone cannot say, a host requirement, when a value takes effect. The card's own `hint` speaks for the whole card; this one is bound to the field it qualifies.

rebuild.description: This value only takes effect after the sandbox is rebuilt, because it rides the image overlay. Shown as a chip beside the label: two switches side by side, identical in every visible way, can otherwise cost five seconds or five minutes with no way to tell which.

options.description: Turns the field into a select.

when.description: Only show this field while a condition over the answers already given holds: `auth == 'key'`, `provider in ['ipsec', 'fortinet']`, `!advanced`. Supports `&&`, `||`, `!`, comparisons and `in`.

value.description: A fixed value baked into the config rather than asked for: how a card pins its discriminator (platform="reddit", provider="stripe"). Renders as nothing.

totp.description: This field holds a TOTP seed, the base32 key or otpauth:// URI a service shows when enrolling an authenticator app. Declare it with `secret: true`. Unlike an ordinary secret it never enters the agent's environment: the daemon mints the six-digit codes on demand and only those cross.

kind.description: The kind of connection it names: `device`, `exit`, `identity`, `cli`.

provider.description: For a kind several cards share, the card it was added from: a cli card's `provider` (`imap`), a site's `platform`.

connection.description: Answer this field by picking one of the owner's existing connections of this kind, by name, instead of typing the name. The empty choice is what leaving the field empty means, labelled with `placeholder`; with none of that kind connected, the field says so. The value stored is the connection's name, and the sandbox refuses a name that is not one.

keyValue.description: Render it as rows of a name and a value with add and remove, for a block of `KEY=VALUE` lines (an agent's environment). What is stored is those lines, the same text a `multiline` box holds. With `secret: true` the values are masked.

subject.description: The request's subject, attribute by attribute, as templates over the other fields (`${organization}`). An attribute that comes out empty is left out; letters with diacritics are written without them.

request.description: A non-secret `multiline` field the request itself is kept in, so the card shows it again later; the form draws it inside this one rather than as a box of its own.

keyRequest.description: This secret field holds a private key the sandbox generates and keeps (RSA 2048): the form shows a PKCS#10 certificate signing request for it to copy or download, and the key itself never reaches the browser. For a service that issues a certificate from a request, which the card then takes in another field.

signIn.description: Fill this field with a sign-in button instead of a text box, and the refresh token lands here for Save to store, with nobody pasting a token. `google`: the platform's own OAuth client runs the consent screen, and the card's CLI trades the token for access tokens through the daemon's `POST /capabilities/{id}/oauth-access`, since the client secret stays on the platform. `microsoft`: the sandbox runs the device-code sign-in the card's `refreshToken.deviceCode` declares, against the card's own app. Only on the secret field the card's `refreshToken` names.

channel.description: Facts about the platform this card reaches: its one-message limit, whether your backend publishes approved posts there itself and to which targets, and what a publishing turn should know about posting there. A post's `platform` names this card's id.

messageLimit.description: The longest one message may be on this platform, in JavaScript string length (UTF-16 code units). The approvals inbox counts a post against it, and your own gateway splits a reply there. Absent: no known cap.

publish.description: Your backend publishes this platform's approved posts itself (`api.approvals.publish`), handed over by the approvals queue only after the person's yes was matched and spent, instead of an agent turn driving the logged-in browser. Needs `server`.

target.description: The targets your backend can address, as a regular expression a post's whole `target` must match (`^\\d{5,}$` for a channel id). A post with another target, or with attachments, goes to an agent turn instead.

posting.description: What an agent turn publishing an approved post on this platform should know beyond its skill, said once in the turn's brief: how a reply nests, what a target means here.

flow.description: Which kind of path this is: `team-chat` (people's messages, both ways), `email-imap` (mail read from a server), `email-smtp` (mail sent through one), `connector` (whatever the agent chose to send).

operator.description: Who runs the service, as its terms name them (`Discord Inc.`). Absent: the office is asked.

region.description: Where the operator says it processes the data (`US`, `EU`, `EU/US`), only where it publishes one.

thirdCountry.description: True when the operator processes the data outside the European Economic Area, which makes this a transfer to a third country.

hosts.description: Every host data is sent to on this path, beyond the card's `hosts`: a realtime gateway, a file CDN.

hostField.description: The card's field naming the server this path reaches (an IMAP card's `host`). The path exists only once that field is filled in.

processors.description: Where a card of this kind sends people's data, one entry per path out, for the Data protection page and the documents it drafts. Absent: one generic connector path over the card's `hosts`.

env.description: The environment the agent's shell gets, as value templates over the fields: `${field}` substitutes, `${field:uri}` percent-encodes. Each name is suffixed per instance.

skill.description: Checkout-relative SKILL.md teaching the agent this tool. `${id}` in it is replaced with the instance name at apply time.

fragment.description: A Dockerfile fragment holding the client binary this tool needs (psql, mysql, whisper).

pack.description: A sandbox feature pack name (whisper, llamacpp, browser, …) supplying this tool. Preferred over `fragment`: an image that already bakes the pack needs no rebuild, and there is no copy to drift.

probe.description: One authenticated request that tests this card's settings before they are saved, so a wrong token or an unreachable host is answered on the form rather than by a card that says 'not connected' afterwards. For a service not spoken to over HTTP, `connect` names the protocol the daemon dials it with instead of `url`.

oauth.description: Trade the card's refresh token, or its app's client secret, for an access token before the request, sent as `Authorization: Bearer`. For Microsoft's identity platform the request goes to the Graph cloud paired with the token endpoint's host, whatever host `url` names.

tokenUrl.description: The token endpoint, templated like `url`. Only Microsoft identity platform hosts are served today.

form.description: The grant's form fields, templated like `url`; a field that comes out empty is left out. `grant_type` is `refresh_token` (a delegated sign-in: nothing to test until someone has signed in) or `client_credentials` (an app's own secret, with `scope` naming the resource's `.default`).

url.description: The URL to call, as a template over the fields: `${field}` substitutes, `${field:uri}` percent-encodes. Same spelling as `env`.

headers.description: The request headers, templated the same way: `{"Authorization": "Bearer ${token}"}`.

identity.description: A dotted path into the JSON answer naming who the caller is ("login", "user.name"), so success can say which account answered.

ok.description: A dotted path into the JSON answer that must hold `true` for the answer to count ("ok"), for a service that answers 200 either way and says in the body whether the call worked. Anything else fails the test, naming the answer's `error` code.

insecure.description: Accept a self-signed certificate, for a service whose local install ships one (Obsidian's Local REST API).

connect.description: What to dial. `tcp`: only that something accepts a connection there. `postgres` and `mysql`: sign in to the database (TLS when the server offers it, as their command-line clients do) and name the server's version. `imap`: sign in with LOGIN, over implicit TLS on 993 and STARTTLS where offered elsewhere; with no password it only checks the greeting.

user.description: Who to sign in as, templated.

database.description: The database to open, for `postgres` and `mysql`; the one a success names.

refreshToken.description: This card's credential is a delegated OAuth refresh token the extension's own CLI or process obtains and rotates. They store it through `POST /capabilities/{id}/oauth-token` (an extension process also needs that route in `permissions.daemon`) instead of printing it for someone to paste.

field.description: The secret field the refresh token is kept in.

boundTo.description: Fields a token is only good for as filled in at sign-in (tenant, client, cloud, access level); a token arriving after one of them changed is refused.

deviceCode.description: How the form signs in on its own (RFC 8628 device authorization), for the field declaring `signIn: "microsoft"`: the sandbox asks for a code, shows it with the provider's page, waits for the person there, and fills the field. The CLI's own sign-in stays for the agent.

when.description: Only while this condition over the answers holds does the button stand in for the field (`!clientSecret`: an app with a secret of its own brings its own token). Otherwise the field stays a box to paste into.

authorizeUrl.description: The device authorization endpoint, templated like `probe.url`: `https://${authority}/${tenantId:uri}/oauth2/v2.0/devicecode`.

tokenUrl.description: The token endpoint the sandbox polls until the person finishes, templated the same way. Only Microsoft identity platform hosts are served today.

clientId.description: The public client the sign-in runs as, templated: `${clientId}`.

scope.description: What the sign-in asks for, templated: one string, or a list whose first entry with no `when`, or a `when` that holds, is asked (read permissions alone for a read-only card). On Microsoft's identity platform a scope naming `https://graph.microsoft.com/` is asked of the Graph paired with the token endpoint's cloud.

hosts.description: The hosts this card's credential is meant for, as templates over the fields like `env` (`api.github.com`, `*.githubusercontent.com`, `${url}`); a value that comes out as a URL counts as its host. The sandbox limits the credential's `{{secret:…}}` reference to them by default, so a use aimed anywhere else asks a person first. The owner can change or lift the list on the Secrets view.

broker.description: Route the credential through the sandbox's credential gateway instead of handing it to the agent: per upstream, the variable carrying the gateway's address and how the credential is attached, plus optional method and path rules. Every `env` variable whose template names a secret field then holds an inert placeholder. Declare it on every card whose service is spoken to over HTTP.

upstream.description: The service's base URL, a template over the fields like `env` (`https://api.github.com`, `${url}`). What is sent to this route's gateway address goes here and nowhere else.

env.description: The variable the agent's shell finds this route's gateway address in (`GITHUB_API_URL`), suffixed per instance like `env`. Naming one of `env`'s own variables (`GITLAB_URL`) points it at the gateway instead of the service, so a skill written against it needs no change.

headers.description: The headers that carry the credential, templated over the fields (`{"authorization": "Bearer ${token}"}`). The gateway sets them on every request it forwards, replacing any the agent sent under the same name.

basic.description: HTTP Basic credentials, templated over the fields, for a service that takes them (git over HTTPS: `x-access-token` and `${token}`).

form.description: Fields the gateway sets in a request's url-encoded form body, templated over the fields, for a service that takes its credential there: an OAuth token exchange's `client_secret` or `refresh_token`. What the exchange answers (a short-lived access token) is the agent's to use; the long-lived secret never is.

pathPrefix.description: A path the gateway puts before the agent's own, templated over the fields, for a service that takes its credential in the path (Telegram's `/bot${token}`).

git.description: This upstream serves git over HTTP: the agent's git is pointed at the gateway for it (`url.<gateway>.insteadOf`), so a clone, fetch or push needs no credential in the agent's hands.

rules.description: What the credential may do, checked in order against each request the gateway forwards; the first rule covering a request decides, and one no rule covers is allowed. The owner's own rules for a card replace these.

methods.description: The HTTP methods it covers (`DELETE`, `PUT`); absent covers every method.

paths.description: The paths it covers, below the route's upstream: `*` matches one segment, `**` any number of them (`/repos/*/*/hooks/**`). Absent covers every path.

action.description: `allow` forwards it, `ask` holds it on a card for the owner, `deny` refuses it.

why.description: One line on what the rule protects, shown on the card or in the refusal.

actions.description: The outward actions this card's requests perform (send, edit, react), checked in order against each request the gateway sees; the first that covers it names it. The gateway records each request of a card that declares any in Activity (one no action covers as `api.call`) and holds it to the owner's action rules for `<card id>.<action>`.

action.description: The action's key below the card's id (`message.send`, `reaction.add`): the sandbox names it `<card id>.<action>`, which is the key the owner's action rules (Guardrails) are written under.

methods.description: The HTTP methods that perform it; absent is every method.

paths.description: The paths that perform it, below the route's upstream, in the rules' globs: `*` one segment, `**` any number (`/channels/*/messages`). Absent is every path.

read.description: This action only reads. It is recorded and held to a rule written for it like any other, but Guardrails does not offer it: a rule there would hold the bot reading its own channel.

channel.description: Where the request names the channel, chat or recipient it acts on, for its Activity row.

field.description: A top-level field of the request's JSON, url-encoded or multipart body, else of its query (`channel`, `chat_id`).

after.description: The path segment that follows this one (`channels` reads `123` from `/channels/123/messages`).

content.description: Where the request carries what it says, for its Activity row. A JSON body without that field is recorded whole; a file upload never is.

field.description: A top-level field of the request's body (`text`, `content`).

from.description: The card's status is whatever this extension's listener last reported for it.

pairingSteps.description: Where a person types the pairing code the listener reports, as the card says it: "Type this code <pairingSteps>."

status.description: Take this card's status from your listener's report (`POST /listeners/<provider>/status`, its `connections` and `pairing`), for a card whose settings anyone could type but only the gateway knows whether they work.

commandActions.description: The outward actions this card's command-line tools perform (`whatsapp send` sends a message), for a tool that reaches its service some other way than the gateway. Each is offered on Guardrails as `<card id>.<action>`. The sandbox refuses a command the owner's rule denies or holds before it runs and records it in Activity once it ends, unless the card's backend carries it out (`gatedBy: "backend"`), which then asks the outward-action door instead.

action.description: The action's key below the card's id (`message.send`, `reaction.add`): the sandbox names it `<card id>.<action>`, which is the key the owner's action rules (Guardrails) are written under.

command.description: The program and the words that select the command (`["whatsapp", "send"]`), matched at the start of an invocation.

read.description: This action only reads. It is recorded and held to a rule written for it like any other, but Guardrails does not offer it: a rule there would hold the bot reading its own channel.

channel.description: The argument naming the chat or recipient, for its Activity row.

arg.description: The argument's position after the command's own words, counted from 0.

content.description: The argument carrying what it says, for its Activity row.

arg.description: The argument's position after the command's own words, counted from 0.

rest.description: Take every argument from there on, joined by spaces (a message typed unquoted).

gatedBy.description: Who holds the command to the owner's action rule. `sandbox` (the default): the command guard refuses a command the rule denies or holds before it runs, and the turn records it in Activity once it ends. `backend`: the card's own backend carries the action out and asks the sandbox's outward-action door first (`POST /capabilities/{id}/outward-action`), which decides, records it in Activity and turns a hold into an approvals item the backend performs once a person says yes; the command guard lets the command run, so a held send reaches the door that drafts its approval.

unruled.description: What the action comes to while no action rule names it. `allow` (the default) lets it go. `hold` waits for the owner's yes until a rule says otherwise: the command guard refuses it with the way to draft an approval, or, for `gatedBy: "backend"`, the outward-action door drafts it. Guardrails shows it as the action's default. Declarations of one action that differ hold it if any says `hold`.

selfGated.description: Deprecated since 2.52.0: declare `gatedBy: "backend"` and `unruled: "hold"`, which is how `true` is still read (an `unruled` beside it wins).

mcp.description: Deprecated: declare `contributes.tools` with `perCard` naming this card instead, and serve the tools with `api.tools.serve`. A path in this extension's backend (`server`) answering MCP over Streamable HTTP; every turn granted a card of this kind gets it as a server named by the card's id, each request arriving at `<path>/<card id>`.

power.sentence: serves MCP tools to the agent for each "${catalog.name}" card

art.description: This extension's own mark, as a complete SVG document inline: the tier an author controls fully. Give it a viewBox and let it fill its own square edge to edge; it is drawn as the tile, not as a glyph on a plate. Kept as readable SVG text (not base64) so a registry reviewer can see what they are publishing, drawn inert so it cannot script the page, and capped at 4 KB. Anything that does not parse as SVG falls back to `logo`, then `icon`, then initials.

logo.description: A simple-icons slug, fetched from a CDN: right for standing in for somebody else's product. Add a "/<hex>" suffix to force a colour for a mark that vanishes against the surface it lands on. Unreachable in an offline sandbox, so it falls back to `icon`, then to initials.

icon.description: A name from the host's own icon set, drawn when no simple-icons slug fits. It ships in the image, follows the theme and costs no request: what actually carries a first-party extension. An unknown name falls back to initials rather than to a hole.

description.description: ONE LINE: aim for 60 characters or fewer. The grid clamps it at two lines in a narrow pane, so a paragraph here is a paragraph the reader gets truncated. Everything longer belongs in `hint`.

hint.description: The paragraph, shown under the add form and searched from the catalog, so the words that identify this card to someone hunting for it ("webauthn", "socket mode") belong here even when the tile cannot show them.

guide.description: The walkthrough the install dialog renders for getting the credential this card asks for.

links.description: Links each connected card of this kind offers on its row, for a step taken on the service's own site after connecting (inviting a bot to a server). A template naming a secret field is refused: the editor is never shown one.

label.description: What the link says on the connected card: "Add to your server".

url.description: The address, templated over the card's non-secret fields like `env`: `${field}` substitutes, `${field:uri}` percent-encodes. Offered only once every field it names holds a value.

secret.description: Mask it, and never echo it back.

advanced.description: Fold this field behind the form's Advanced disclosure: for answers whose default is right for nearly everyone. The disclosure opens by itself while any advanced field holds a non-default value, so an edit never hides live settings.

boolean.description: Render it as a switch, carrying "on"/"off". For an opt-in EXTRA rather than a decision: a two-option picker says the same thing but presents a choice the user must make to proceed, sized like the required fields around it. A switch always holds a value, so a field like this never blocks a submit.

hint.description: Shown on hover behind an (i) beside the label, never as text under the control: for what the label alone cannot say, a host requirement, when a value takes effect. The card's own `hint` speaks for the whole card; this one is bound to the field it qualifies.

rebuild.description: This value only takes effect after the sandbox is rebuilt, because it rides the image overlay. Shown as a chip beside the label: two switches side by side, identical in every visible way, can otherwise cost five seconds or five minutes with no way to tell which.

options.description: Turns the field into a select.

when.description: Only show this field while a condition over the answers already given holds: `auth == 'key'`, `provider in ['ipsec', 'fortinet']`, `!advanced`. Supports `&&`, `||`, `!`, comparisons and `in`.

value.description: A fixed value baked into the config rather than asked for: how a card pins its discriminator (platform="reddit", provider="stripe"). Renders as nothing.

totp.description: This field holds a TOTP seed, the base32 key or otpauth:// URI a service shows when enrolling an authenticator app. Declare it with `secret: true`. Unlike an ordinary secret it never enters the agent's environment: the daemon mints the six-digit codes on demand and only those cross.

kind.description: The kind of connection it names: `device`, `exit`, `identity`, `cli`.

provider.description: For a kind several cards share, the card it was added from: a cli card's `provider` (`imap`), a site's `platform`.

connection.description: Answer this field by picking one of the owner's existing connections of this kind, by name, instead of typing the name. The empty choice is what leaving the field empty means, labelled with `placeholder`; with none of that kind connected, the field says so. The value stored is the connection's name, and the sandbox refuses a name that is not one.

keyValue.description: Render it as rows of a name and a value with add and remove, for a block of `KEY=VALUE` lines (an agent's environment). What is stored is those lines, the same text a `multiline` box holds. With `secret: true` the values are masked.

subject.description: The request's subject, attribute by attribute, as templates over the other fields (`${organization}`). An attribute that comes out empty is left out; letters with diacritics are written without them.

request.description: A non-secret `multiline` field the request itself is kept in, so the card shows it again later; the form draws it inside this one rather than as a box of its own.

keyRequest.description: This secret field holds a private key the sandbox generates and keeps (RSA 2048): the form shows a PKCS#10 certificate signing request for it to copy or download, and the key itself never reaches the browser. For a service that issues a certificate from a request, which the card then takes in another field.

signIn.description: Fill this field with a sign-in button instead of a text box, and the refresh token lands here for Save to store, with nobody pasting a token. `google`: the platform's own OAuth client runs the consent screen, and the card's CLI trades the token for access tokens through the daemon's `POST /capabilities/{id}/oauth-access`, since the client secret stays on the platform. `microsoft`: the sandbox runs the device-code sign-in the card's `refreshToken.deviceCode` declares, against the card's own app. Only on the secret field the card's `refreshToken` names.

channel.description: Facts about the platform this card reaches: its one-message limit, whether your backend publishes approved posts there itself and to which targets, and what a publishing turn should know about posting there. A post's `platform` names this card's id.

messageLimit.description: The longest one message may be on this platform, in JavaScript string length (UTF-16 code units). The approvals inbox counts a post against it, and your own gateway splits a reply there. Absent: no known cap.

publish.description: Your backend publishes this platform's approved posts itself (`api.approvals.publish`), handed over by the approvals queue only after the person's yes was matched and spent, instead of an agent turn driving the logged-in browser. Needs `server`.

target.description: The targets your backend can address, as a regular expression a post's whole `target` must match (`^\\d{5,}$` for a channel id). A post with another target, or with attachments, goes to an agent turn instead.

posting.description: What an agent turn publishing an approved post on this platform should know beyond its skill, said once in the turn's brief: how a reply nests, what a target means here.

flow.description: Which kind of path this is: `team-chat` (people's messages, both ways), `email-imap` (mail read from a server), `email-smtp` (mail sent through one), `connector` (whatever the agent chose to send).

operator.description: Who runs the service, as its terms name them (`Discord Inc.`). Absent: the office is asked.

region.description: Where the operator says it processes the data (`US`, `EU`, `EU/US`), only where it publishes one.

thirdCountry.description: True when the operator processes the data outside the European Economic Area, which makes this a transfer to a third country.

hosts.description: Every host data is sent to on this path, beyond the card's `hosts`: a realtime gateway, a file CDN.

hostField.description: The card's field naming the server this path reaches (an IMAP card's `host`). The path exists only once that field is filled in.

processors.description: Where a card of this kind sends people's data, one entry per path out, for the Data protection page and the documents it drafts. Absent: one generic connector path over the card's `hosts`.

loginUrl.description: What the sign-in window opens; the profile it persists IS the credential. Optional so one card can be the generic one that asks for the URL on its form instead, but a card must either pin this or declare a field that supplies it, or the window opens on nothing.

homeUrl.description: Where that same profile opens once it HAS a session: the owner's own hands on the connected browser. Separate from loginUrl because for some platforms the login lives on another site entirely (YouTube signs in at accounts.google.com).

skill.description: Checkout-relative SKILL.md teaching the agent this site's actions: rendered once per site, all its connected accounts on one roster (`${accounts}`), the core tool note at `${tools}`.

subject.description: The request's subject, attribute by attribute, as templates over the other fields (`${organization}`). An attribute that comes out empty is left out; letters with diacritics are written without them.

request.description: A non-secret `multiline` field the request itself is kept in, so the card shows it again later; the form draws it inside this one rather than as a box of its own.

flow.description: Which kind of path this is: `team-chat` (people's messages, both ways), `email-imap` (mail read from a server), `email-smtp` (mail sent through one), `connector` (whatever the agent chose to send).

operator.description: Who runs the service, as its terms name them (`Discord Inc.`). Absent: the office is asked.

skill.description: Checkout-relative SKILL.md teaching the agent to work on this phone.

art.description: This extension's own mark, as a complete SVG document inline: the tier an author controls fully. logo.description: A simple-icons slug, fetched from a CDN: right for standing in for somebody else's product. Add a "/<hex>" suffix to force a colour for a mark that vanishes against the surface it lands on. Unreachable in an offline sandbox, so it falls back to `icon`, then to initials.

icon.description: A name from the host's own icon set, drawn when no simple-icons slug fits. It ships in the image, follows the theme and costs no request: what actually carries a first-party extension. An unknown name falls back to initials rather than to a hole.

description.description: ONE LINE: aim for 60 characters or fewer. The grid clamps it at two lines in a narrow pane, so a paragraph here is a paragraph the reader gets truncated. Everything longer belongs in `hint`.

hint.description: The paragraph, shown under the add form and searched from the catalog, so the words that identify this card to someone hunting for it ("webauthn", "socket mode") belong here even when the tile cannot show them.

guide.description: The walkthrough the install dialog renders for getting the credential this card asks for.

links.description: Links each connected card of this kind offers on its row, for a step taken on the service's own site after connecting (inviting a bot to a server). A template naming a secret field is refused: the editor is never shown one.

label.description: What the link says on the connected card: "Add to your server".

url.description: The address, templated over the card's non-secret fields like `env`: `${field}` substitutes, `${field:uri}` percent-encodes. Offered only once every field it names holds a value.

secret.description: Mask it, and never echo it back.

advanced.description: Fold this field behind the form's Advanced disclosure: for answers whose default is right for nearly everyone. The disclosure opens by itself while any advanced field holds a non-default value, so an edit never hides live settings.

boolean.description: Render it as a switch, carrying "on"/"off". For an opt-in EXTRA rather than a decision: a two-option picker says the same thing but presents a choice the user must make to proceed, sized like the required fields around it. A switch always holds a value, so a field like this never blocks a submit.

hint.description: Shown on hover behind an (i) beside the label, never as text under the control: for what the label alone cannot say, a host requirement, when a value takes effect. The card's own `hint` speaks for the whole card; this one is bound to the field it qualifies.

rebuild.description: This value only takes effect after the sandbox is rebuilt, because it rides the image overlay. Shown as a chip beside the label: two switches side by side, identical in every visible way, can otherwise cost five seconds or five minutes with no way to tell which.

options.description: Turns the field into a select.

when.description: Only show this field while a condition over the answers already given holds: `auth == 'key'`, `provider in ['ipsec', 'fortinet']`, `!advanced`. Supports `&&`, `||`, `!`, comparisons and `in`.

value.description: A fixed value baked into the config rather than asked for: how a card pins its discriminator (platform="reddit", provider="stripe"). Renders as nothing.

totp.description: This field holds a TOTP seed, the base32 key or otpauth:// URI a service shows when enrolling an authenticator app. Declare it with `secret: true`. Unlike an ordinary secret it never enters the agent's environment: the daemon mints the six-digit codes on demand and only those cross.

kind.description: The kind of connection it names: `device`, `exit`, `identity`, `cli`.

provider.description: For a kind several cards share, the card it was added from: a cli card's `provider` (`imap`), a site's `platform`.

connection.description: Answer this field by picking one of the owner's existing connections of this kind, by name, instead of typing the name. power.sentence: a ${kind} capability card "${catalog.name}"

capabilities.description: Capability cards this pack adds to the "+" grid: a connected CLI tool, a site the agent acts on as the owner through the shared browser, an operating system pack, a browser family the owner connects their own copy of, or a preset over a core kind. The card and its form are data here; the machinery that acts on them is core, which is why a card may only name one of these five kinds.

provider.description: The slug this source's automation triggers fire on.

events.description: The event types this source can fire, with the wording the automation editor offers them under. The daemon accepts no others.

strangers.description: Set when anyone on the internet can reach this source without the owner adding them (a chat on a public page, a crash reporter), which holds its wakes to the owner's floor for strangers: `visitor`, someone talking with an assistant; `report`, a stranger's report setting work going, held for approval unless the owner says otherwise. Absent: its senders are people the owner connected, held to the floor for a team chat message.

power.sentence: anyone on the internet can wake an agent through its "${provider}" listener

mentionLabel.description: Only for a source whose message events distinguish being addressed. Absent ⇒ the editor offers no mention-only filter, rather than inventing semantics you did not promise.

hint.description: The sentence under the input, for a filter whose empty case is easy to get wrong.

channel.description: The primary narrowing filter, a channel, a room, a repo.

branchField.description: A second narrowing axis, for a source whose events carry one: a pipeline's git ref, so a trigger can say "the branch that ships" rather than "every agent's every failure".

hint.description: The sentence under the input, for a filter whose empty case is easy to get wrong.

sender.description: How this source names a sender, and where a person finds that id. Declaring it promises that `author.id` is an identity the service vouches for, not a name the sender typed; absent ⇒ the editor offers no sender rules on this source.

hint.description: The sentence under the input, for a filter whose empty case is easy to get wrong.

senderGroup.description: How this source names a sender's group, for a source whose messages carry `author.groups` (a Discord role). Absent ⇒ rules match ids only.

hint.description: The sentence under the input, for a filter whose empty case is easy to get wrong.

starterPrompt.description: The first prompt a new automation on this source is prefilled with. You own the payload vocabulary, so you own the prompt that explains it.

automation.description: How the generic automation editor presents this source: its name, its filters, and the prompt it starts people on.

power.sentence: a realtime listener provider "${provider}"

listener.description: A realtime event source this extension supplies, so automations can trigger on it. One declaration feeds both halves: the daemon accepts these event types and serves this provider's control surface, and the automation editor derives its source picker, filters and starter prompt from it, so a newly installed listener is configurable without a matching app release.

id.description: Prefills the automation name, and is what "does one of these exist already" is asked by, so spell it as an id, not as prose.

logo.description: A simple-icons slug for the card.

icon.description: A name from the host's icon set, drawn when no simple-icons slug fits.

requires.description: Capability providers that make this template work: any one connected is enough (fixing CI rides github or gitlab). Omitted ⇒ nothing to connect, so it is always offered.

tz.description: Which clock the cron's times mean, as a zone name. Absent: the sandbox's own.

afterSessions.description: Fire only once this many new sessions have run since the last wake.

dailyMax.description: How many webhook calls a day may wake it.

signature.description: Require the sender's signature: its scheme, and the name of the sandbox secret holding the signing secret.

trigger.description: What wakes it. Checked against the real trigger schema when the daemon builds the catalogue, so a template can never offer one that would be refused.

guard.description: A condition that must hold before the turn runs: what makes a template safe to leave switched on.

source.description: A ready-made check instead of a guard: `{ kind: "url", url, select? }`, the sandbox's own, or a kind an enabled extension declares in `watchKinds`, its parameters beside `kind`.

fireOn.description: Fire on every passing check, or only when what it saw changed.

until.description: Switch it off the first time it fires.

target.description: What a passing check sets off: a new agent (the default), only a notification, or (`extension`) a handler of this extension's own backend, which only this extension can save.

holdForSeconds.description: Wait this long and coalesce repeats, rather than firing on every event.

prompt.description: The turn this starts. You own the trigger's payload vocabulary, so you own the prompt that reads it.

setup.description: What the user must do themselves before this can work.

offer.description: Absent ⇒ it waits in the gallery, where you go once you know what you want. `create` puts a card on the page that makes it, switched off, in one click. `configure` puts one there that opens the dialog prefilled, for a template that cannot work unconfigured. Both are for what a user would never think to go looking for: mark everything as offered and you have rebuilt the gallery with extra steps.

chore.description: Whether what this makes watches THIS codebase rather than the outside world. Declared rather than read off the trigger: a nightly dependency sweep and a nightly Stripe poll are both schedules.

automationTemplates.description: Starting points this pack offers in the automation composer, a trigger, a prompt written for that trigger's payload, and whatever guard makes it safe to leave on. Declared by whoever knows the service rather than by the composer, so they appear when your pack is installed and disappear with it. Pure prefill: creating one makes an ordinary automation.

id.description: The kind's id, which an automation's source names as `kind`. Keep it once shipped: a stored automation names it.

label.description: What the composer's chip says: a few words, like `npm package`.

icon.description: A name from the host's icon set for the chip.

logo.description: A simple-icons slug, drawn where a logo fits better than an icon.

description.description: One sentence under the chips on what the check looks at and when it passes.

sentence.description: What one source of this kind watches, in a few words, for the automation's row, its approval card and the wake: `{key}` puts a parameter in, and a `[…]` segment is left out when a parameter it names is absent or off, like `GitHub releases of {repo}[ (prereleases too){prereleases}]`. A switch puts nothing in: it only keeps its segment.

key.description: The parameter's name as the automation stores it, beside `kind`: what `--with <key>=<value>` sets on the command line.

label.description: The box's label in the composer.

type.description: `text` (the default): a line of text, stored as typed. `switch`: on or off, stored as `true` only when on.

required.description: Whether a source of this kind must carry it. A switch is never required.

placeholder.description: An example value, shown in the empty box.

hint.description: One sentence on what it changes, behind the field's (i).

pattern.description: A regular expression a text value must match, checked when the automation is saved, in the composer and by the command.

patternHint.description: What a value that matches looks like, said when one does not: `owner/name`.

maxLength.description: The longest a text value may be. Absent means 2000 characters.

fields.description: Its parameters, in the order the composer draws them.

capabilities.description: Ids of this extension's own capability cards whose credential-gateway addresses each check is handed, as the automation's role reaches them: a GitHub card for a private repository's releases. Never a credential itself.

power.sentence: its backend checks "${label}" watches for the sandbox's automations

watchKinds.description: Ready-made checks an automation can name instead of a guard command: a package's version, a service's newest release. Your backend answers each check (`api.checks.serve(id, handler)`), and the sandbox runs it on the automation's schedule with no shell and no model, firing only when it passes or when what it saw changed. The composer, the `automations` command and the approval card draw each kind from this declaration. Needs a `server` bundle.

id.description: The job's id: what the owner's choice of setup is stored under, and what a run this extension starts names as `job` on POST /agent. Keep it once shipped: a stored choice names it. An id the sandbox's own jobs or an earlier extension already use is not taken.

label.description: What the settings page calls the job, in the owner's words: `Pipeline fixes`.

explanation.description: One sentence under the label on what starts the job, saying more than the label does: `The agent started by Fix on a failed pipeline.`

icon.description: A name from the host's icon set for the job's chip. Absent draws a wrench.

setup.description: The setup the job is suggested: where a sandbox that never placed its jobs runs it, and where the settings page puts it when the owner places it again. What the work needs, not what it costs today. Absent is `medium`.

modelRoles.description: The jobs this extension starts agent runs for, each of which the owner puts on a model setup in Sandbox ▸ Agent ▸ Models beside the sandbox's own: a run you start through `POST /agent` names its job as `job`, and runs on that setup's model when it names none of its own (an id the sandbox's own table held until 2026-11-26 may ride as `runRole`, which a sandbox from before reads too). Switching the extension off hides its jobs on that page and keeps the owner's choices for them.

power.sentence: puts its shipped tools on the agent's PATH

bin.description: A checkout-relative directory of executables the daemon puts on the agent's PATH every turn, how you ship the agent a command-line tool. The files are the approved code themselves: they ride the pinned checkout, and the daemon only adds the directory to PATH.

perCard.description: The id of one of this extension's `cli` capability cards. Every turn granted a card of that kind gets one server named by the card's id, handed that card's settings (secrets included) with each call. Absent ⇒ one server for the extension, named by its `name`, in every turn while the extension is enabled.

process.description: A process from `contributes.processes`, declared with `port: "auto"`, that answers MCP over Streamable HTTP at `path` on its port. Absent ⇒ your `server` bundle serves the tools.

path.description: Where the MCP endpoint answers, without a leading or trailing slash: on the process's port, or in your backend's own namespace when your `server` bundle speaks MCP itself. Absent with no `process` ⇒ the host serves what `api.tools.serve` returns, which is what you want: the host owns the transport, the deadlines and the card lookup. With `perCard`, a request arrives at `<path>/<card id>`.

power.sentence: gives the agent MCP tools${perCard?, one server for each "${perCard}" card:}

tools.description: Tools for the agent, as an MCP server the daemon mounts into every turn and every runtime (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, ACP agents). Serve them from your `server` bundle with `api.tools.serve((card) => [...])`, or from a declared process's port. Replaces an agent plugin's `.mcp.json`, which only Claude Code read.

path.description: Where it answers, under /door/<id>/: segments joined by "/", each a lowercase word or a lone `*` for any one segment, e.g. "hook", "*/report".

methods.description: The methods it answers; anything else is refused before your backend hears of it.

automation.description: The path's first `*` names an automation listening on this extension's own listener provider: one that is not there answers 404 and one switched off 409, its `allowedOrigins` are the list `origins` checks, its door key is what `key` admits, and the day's ceiling is counted per automation.

origins.description: `listed`: a browser's Origin must be on the automation's allowed origins, or the call is refused (403); needs `automation`. `any` or absent: no Origin is checked, as for a provider's webhook.

key.description: A caller with no Origin to check (an app, a server) may present the automation's door key instead, as `?key=` or `Authorization: Bearer`; needs `automation` and `origins: "listed"`. The key itself never reaches your backend.

keyFromBrowsers.description: (2026-11-26) An automation that opts in (its trigger's `keyFromBrowsers`) lets its door key admit a browser whose Origin is not on its list too; needs `key`. The owner opts each automation in, off by default, since a key in a public page is anyone's to copy: the minute's window and the day's ceiling are then what bound it.

signature.description: Refuse anything not signed by the sender with the named secret (and, for a timestamped scheme, sent within five minutes); a redelivery of a call already taken is answered without reaching your backend.

scheme.description: Which provider's signing scheme the sender uses.

secret.description: The name of the sandbox secret holding the signing secret, which the owner sets; its value never reaches your backend.

turnstile.description: Refuse a call without a Cloudflare Turnstile token the sandbox verifies with Cloudflare under the named secret: the page renders the widget with its site key (public, yours to serve) and sends the token it gets as `x-intentic-turnstile`. A token is good once.

secret.description: The name of the sandbox secret holding the Cloudflare Turnstile secret key, which the owner sets; its value never reaches your backend.

proofOfWork.description: Refuse a call without a solved challenge: the caller fetches one at GET /door/<id>/~challenge?caller=<its id> and sends `x-intentic-pow: <salt>:<nonce>` and `x-intentic-pow-caller: <its id>`.

rate.description: Calls a minute one caller (by address) may make before 429; 30 when absent.

dailyMax.description: Calls a day it takes in all (per automation, for an automation's route) before 429; 1000 when absent. `"none"` (2026-11-26) counts no day at all, for a route that only serves what a page loads (a script, its settings), so a busy site's page views cannot shut it; only a GET-only route may say it, and its minute's window and size still hold.

bodyMax.description: The largest body it takes, in bytes; 65536 when absent, at most 1048576.

power.sentence: anyone on the internet can call its backend at ${methods|, } /${path}${signature? when signed with your secret ${signature.secret}:}

publicRoutes.description: Routes anyone on the internet may call without signing in, served at /door/<id>/<path> and handed to your backend's `api.publicRoutes.serve` handler only after the sandbox's own protections passed the call: its size, a per-minute window and a daily ceiling, an automation's allowed origins or its door key, a proof-of-work challenge, a Cloudflare Turnstile token, a provider's signature, the last two checked against secrets you never see. Each is a power the owner approves.
